Vélez is the founder, chairman, chief executive and — through Rua California Ltd. and the Class B structure — the holder of 74.4% of the votes, so he is simultaneously the person this sweep most needed to clear and the person whose record would have settled the rating on its own. **He came back clean on every axis that could be run, with no adverse record, no undisclosed entity, no political exposure and no cross-linkage.** The one thing the synthesis must carry alongside that is what it does *not* prove: there is no public Cayman register behind it, so "clean" here rests on US securities filings, Brazilian public records and dated media, not on a primary directorship register — and the concentration of control means everything else in this module is judged inside a structure he decides.

**A9-04 — promoter track record at OTHER ventures.** *Not Applicable (no other ventures).* Vélez has founded and controlled exactly one operating business. Before it he was an employee — a partner at Sequoia Capital and, earlier, at Goldman Sachs, Morgan Stanley and General Atlantic — never a controller. There is therefore no second venture at which to test for defaults, enforcement or minority-squeeze history, and this is recorded as a genuine absence of the test's subject rather than as a pass. `[FY25 Form 20-F, Item 6.A; web sweep 2026-09-06]`

**A13-01 — Professional CEO vs promoter-run.** **Amber.** This is a founder-run company with a real professional layer around the founder: a CFO recruited from Visa/Capital One, a CTO from Snap/Google/Amazon, a CRO from HSBC, a Brazil CEO from Itaú/McKinsey, a CDO from Slack and a former central-bank governor running public policy — none of them family. But 74.4% of the votes and both the chair and CEO seats sit with one person, so accountability runs to him rather than through the board. Real depth; no counterweight.

**A13-02 — View on the CEO (operating record).** **Green.** Thirteen years running one business from zero to a NYSE-listed bank across three countries. **No failed or abandoned venture is hidden anywhere in the record**, no venture is presented as a pivot, and no credibility gap between his narrative and the filings was found on the A16-20 test.

**A13-03 — Promoter vintage & involvement.** **Green.** Founder since 2013, continuously executive, with no competing venture and no visible split of attention. He is not an absentee promoter on any reading.

**A13-06 — Family dynamics / succession disputes.** **Green.** No dispute, faction or contested holding. The 20-F states affirmatively that "there are no family relationships among any member of our board of directors or management team," and the only family holdings — his spouse's 1,500,000 Class B and the Junqueira/Pereira trusts — are disclosed by name. Note for `05`: no CEO succession plan is disclosed, but he is 44, so the A1-13 founder-age trigger does not apply.

**A13-07 — Promoter's other material businesses.** **Green.** None competing with, and none transacting with, the listco. Rua California Ltd. is a pure share-holding vehicle, disclosed, with no operating business and no transactions with Nu.

**A13-08 — Sensitive government dealings.** **Amber, and this is the one to watch.** Nu itself has no discretionary government contracts, licence allocations or tender exposure — its revenue is retail consumer finance. But it is a heavily *regulated* business whose economics were reshaped by discretionary central-bank action (Pix, Open Finance), and it has hired the man who took those decisions (§2.4). The dependence is on regulation, not on procurement, and the flag belongs to that fact rather than to any contract.

**A13-09 — Political connect.** **Green as to the controller.** Vélez holds no political office or party role and no material donation or electoral-financing link was found. Recorded separately and not conflated with him: director Luis Alberto Moreno is a disclosed former minister and ambassador holding no current office; director Douglas Leone is a large US political donor (US$1m to America PAC, US$2m to Right for America) with no identified channel to Nu's Brazil/Mexico/Colombia outcomes; and KMP Campos Neto is a former central-bank governor. **None of these is a connection of the controller, and none is written as one.**

Escalate to Material if the CEP matter is reopened or any Brazilian authority opens a new proceeding.

Leone is a Nu director since 2016 and was Global Managing Partner of Sequoia Capital across the years it built and then lost its FTX position, and Sequoia is a defendant in the resulting investor class actions. **No adverse record was found against him personally, he is not a named defendant, and no regulator has acted against him or against Sequoia.** The grade is Minor concerns purely on that linkage, and the second thing the synthesis should carry is unrelated to integrity: eleven outside boards is an overboarding question for `05`.

**Adjudication note — why RF-NET-003 fires for Calderón and not for Leone.** Both are hop-1 links from a register person to an entity with a live problem, so the difference has to be stated rather than assumed. Casas Bahia's *recuperação judicial* is an **admitted insolvency proceeding** — the exact fact the band-(b) trigger names, filed by the debtor itself, quantified at R$17.3bn, three weeks old and unresolved. Sequoia's posture is a **private civil claim, unadjudicated, brought by third parties against an investor that lost US$210m to someone else's fraud**, with no regulator involved, no admission, and no adverse ruling; treating a defendant-investor's pleading-stage exposure as equivalent to an admitted insolvency would inflate an allegation into a fact, which the allegation-≠-conviction rule bans in that direction as firmly as in the other. The linkage is still real, so it still floors the grade at Minor — dropping it because "nothing was found against him personally" is the banned failure in the opposite direction. Flag fired once, on the fact that is admitted.

This is the company Nubank actually is: the 2013-vintage Brazilian payment institution that holds the licences, employs the operations and owns the brand, sitting under a 2016 Cayman holding company that exists to list it. **It is the answer to the founding-year question and it is a disclosed, active, consolidated subsidiary — so the lineage question closes clean rather than opening a predecessor.** Its courts-and-regulator record is `12`'s to run, and this dossier does not claim to have run it.

Lightspark is the answer to the one question triage called its highest-value discovery target, and the answer is anticlimactic in the best way: a US$0.9m liability arising from a publicly announced blockchain-integration partnership with a start-up whose CEO sits on Nu's board, where the money flowed **to** Nu, not from it. **The counterparty is not named in the note, and the honest way to say that is that IAS 24 requires the nature of the relationship and the amounts — both given — and does not require the name, so this is a disclosure-quality observation, not an omission** (§4 classifies it `disclosable-and-disclosed`). The alternative candidate — Lead Bank, whose CEO Jacqueline Reses is also a Nu director — was swept and no Nu transaction was found, which is why the Lightspark identification is stated at high confidence rather than as certainty.

### 2B.8 Uber Technologies, Inc. · Circle Internet Financial, Inc. · Coinbase Global, Inc. — E-B, swept — Grades: **Uber Minor concerns · Circle Clean · Coinbase Minor concerns** (all **E-B depth** — registered charges, founders-at-incorporation, statutory dues, trademark and address axes not assessed)

These three were swept rather than scoped because each carries a known regulatory history that could have propagated an exposure to a Nu director. **None of them does, and the reason in each case is that the link is not live or not material:**

- **Uber Technologies, Inc.** (Pham, CTO April 2013 – May 2020). The 2016 breach of ~57 million user records was concealed by Uber's **Chief Security Officer**, Joe Sullivan, who paid the hackers US$100,000 disguised as a bug bounty while Uber was under FTC investigation; Sullivan was **convicted in October 2022** of obstruction and misprision, sentenced to probation in May 2023, and the conviction was upheld on appeal. **No source located links Thuan Pham to the concealment**, and the matter is a regulatory-obstruction case, not an accounting failure — so A16-18 does not engage for him. Uber's own record earns Minor concerns (a proven concealment on its watch), but **the link is a PAST officer role that ended in May 2020, so it is not a live hop-1 cross-link and it does not float Pham's grade.**
- **Circle Internet Financial, Inc.** (Sands, board 2022–2024). **Nothing adverse found**; the link has ended.
- **Coinbase Global, Inc.** (Moreno, Global Advisory Council since January 2025). Coinbase's SEC litigation is a matter of public record and its own regulatory history earns Minor concerns at entity level, but **Moreno's link is an advisory-council seat, not a directorship or control**, and Coinbase carries no admitted insolvency, active debarment, sanctions match or proven fraud — so neither RF-NET-003 band is met and Moreno's grade is unaffected.

**Why these appear here rather than as a network flag.** All three are the kind of link that a superficial sweep turns into a headline — "Nu director was Uber's CTO during the cover-up," "Nu director sits at Coinbase." Each was checked to its facts and each fails the trigger for a specific, stated reason: no personal involvement, a terminated link, or a fact that is not in either RF-NET-003 band. Recorded, not inflated.

## 3B. Lineage & Phoenix Read (A17-02, A17-03)

Answered in order, on evidence, because a clean answer here has to be a swept answer rather than a silent one.

**1. Does a predecessor exist?** **No predecessor entity exists, and this was established rather than assumed.** Four independent checks were run. (a) *Incorporation vs claim:* Nu Holdings Ltd. was incorporated in the Cayman Islands on 26 February 2016; it claims a 2013 founding. (b) *Previous-names field:* none — Item 16G states affirmatively "We were incorporated as Nu Holdings Ltd. on February 26, 2016," EDGAR shows no former name, and the `"formerly" OR "erstwhile" OR "part of"` sweep returned nothing. (c) *The company's own history pages:* the corporate About URL returned HTTP 403, so the recipe was completed on the company's own IR governance pages and newsroom releases, which say only "founded in 2013 / operations in Brazil 2014, Mexico 2019, Colombia 2020" — **no lineage language of any kind**. (d) *The gap itself:* the three-year difference resolves to **Nu Pagamentos S.A. – Instituição de Pagamento, CNPJ 18.236.120/0001-58, opened 4 June 2013** — a **disclosed, wholly-owned, active, consolidated subsidiary**, named in Item 4 and in the corporate-structure tree, and the registered proprietor of the NUBANK and NU BANK marks. A holding company interposed in 2016 that accurately cites its own disclosed operating subsidiary's start date is the textbook clean case. **A17-02 Green. RF-NET-001 does not fire.**

**2. Did the predecessor fail?** **Not applicable — there is no predecessor, and the 2013-vintage entity is alive.** Nu Pagamentos is active on the Brazilian registry with no insolvency, no *recuperação judicial* or *extrajudicial*, no liquidation and no strike-off, as debtor or as petitioner. The phoenix test's first question therefore returns a hard negative rather than an unknown.

**3. Did assets, brands, staff, address, products or customers continue out of a failed entity?** **No — nothing continued out of anything, because nothing failed.** The brands did not migrate: Nu Pagamentos has owned NUBANK and NU BANK since 2014 and still owns them today, and has litigated as **plaintiff** to protect them (`Nu Pagamentos S.A. v. Nubank.com`, M.D. Fla. 3:21-cv-00507, 2021-05-13; WIPO UDRP D2019-3138). The operating address, licences, staff and customers all remain inside the same live consolidated subsidiary. There is no acquisition of a distressed business, no asset transfer from a resolved entity, and therefore no consideration or legal basis to disclose. **A17-03 Green. RF-NET-002 does not fire.**

**4. Are two live entities trading on the same brand?** **No.** The D-4 corroboration test was run and returns nothing to corroborate: the marks are held by one proprietor inside the group across Latin America and at the USPTO, and no unrelated live company was found using them in an overlapping jurisdiction and class. **A17-04 Green. RF-NET-004 does not fire** — the marks sit inside the consolidated group, not with a controller-linked entity, not under an undisclosed licence, and not in dispute.

**The one honest caveat.** Every leg above rests on the Brazilian CNPJ public record, US trademark and court records, SEC filings and the company's own pages. **It does not rest on the Cayman Islands Registrar of Companies, which publishes no searchable record of company numbers, directors or former names** — so the *Cayman-side* lineage of Nu Holdings Ltd. itself is corroborated only by the company's own affirmative statement in Item 16G and by the absence of any contradicting trace on EDGAR. That is a real coverage limit and it is priced in §6 and in the score, not glossed.

## 5. Scope Boundary & Unexplored Branches (A17-09)

**Breadth budget applied.** The limit used was the standard **25 hop-1 entities / 15 hop-2**. Twenty-five hop-1 entities entered the priority-ordered set (rows 27–51 of the Discovery Register), selected in the fixed order: (1) lineage/predecessor entities → Nu Pagamentos; (2) entities carrying an adverse hit from their scoped pass → **Grupo Casas Bahia, Sequoia Capital, Uber, Coinbase** (this key existed because the scoped pass ran on every candidate *before* selection); (3) entities that transact with the listco or appear in the RPT note → Lightspark, Lead Bank; (4) entities controlled by a Tier-A person → Rua California, Victory Lane and the Junqueira vehicles; (5) entities controlled by Tier-B/C people → the remaining outside boards, ordered by recency of linkage. **Overflow count: approximately 65 named entities** across rows 63–68, listed below. **No lineage/predecessor entity and no Tier-A-controlled entity is in the overflow**, so the declared-overflow cap applies at *People & network integrity max 70* rather than max 60.

**Subsection ceiling.** The output budget allows at most 40 full dossier subsections. **Eleven were used** (six persons, eight entity dossiers of which three are combined in §2B.8). No decision-relevant subject was compressed for space, and no subject was moved to this register because of the subsection ceiling.

## 6. Provenance & Next Data Request

- **Provenance in one sentence.** Of 68 subjects on the Discovery Register, **62 were supplied by the filings, 6 were found independently, and none was user-supplied** — and of the 68, **zero are classified `disclosable-and-omitted`**, so the coverage statistic is high and the disclosure finding is nil.

- **Nominee or independent directorships EXCLUDED from beneficial-interest scope — named.** None were excluded. Every one of the eight independent directors' outside seats is inside the network map and inside the exposure analysis; the eight directors were still swept at Tier C (two escalated to full) for their own integrity, and the four whose seats produced a hit or a live question — **Calderón, Leone, Marcus, Reses** — plus the PEP (**Moreno**) and the roster conflict (**Moritz**) were escalated to a full sweep. The entities excluded from *full-depth entity sweeps* are the fifteen scoped E-B outside boards named in §3 and the sixty-five overflow subjects named in §5, all listed individually.

- **Aggregator conflicts kept in scope and unresolved (A17-10) — named.** Two, and the shorter roster was adopted in neither case:
  1. **Michael J. Moritz KBE — UNRESOLVED and carried forward.** The vendor insider file shows him receiving the **non-employee-director annual RSU grant on 2026-08-07 (25,290 units — identical to Marcus and Moreno) and 1,356 Class A on 2026-08-24 (identical to Piacentini and Sands)**, holding 29,669,166 Class A (0.614%). The **primary sources contradict that**: the AGM 6-K nominee slate (items a–i) names the same nine directors as the FY25 20-F Item 6.A and the company's own IR board page, and he is on none of them. Both readings were kept; he was swept in full and came back clean on his own record; the **category** stays open.
  2. **Roberto de Oliveira Campos Neto — RESOLVED on the primary.** Triage flagged that the CIQ Board Members export lists him as a "Current Board Member" while the 20-F does not. Resolved: the FY25 20-F places him in the **Management Team**, not the board; the AGM 6-K slate does not include him; the company's own IR board page does not list him. **He is a KMP (Executive Vice-Chairman and Global Head of Public Policy), not a director** — and he was kept in scope and swept at Tier A depth regardless.

- **Coverage limits that bind, stated plainly.** The discovery loop **ran** — triage's conditional "loop cannot run" cap does not apply. What did not run: (a) **no primary corporate-registry pull for any Cayman entity** — the Cayman Registrar of Companies publishes no searchable record of company numbers, directors, former names or charges, so the Cayman-side identity of Nu Holdings Ltd., Rua California Ltd. and Victory Lane Ltd. rests on SEC filings and the company's own statements; (b) **no paid court-docket or consolidated-sanctions terminal** — criminal, civil, tribunal and OFAC/UN/EU/Interpol screens were run as dated public searches, which is a screen and not a certified clearance; (c) **fifteen named E-B outside-board entities were scoped, not fully swept**, and ~65 further subjects are declared overflow (§5). Every "clean" claim above traces to a Sweep Log row, and every axis that did not run is marked as not assessed rather than left blank.

- **THE single highest-value next data request.** **Michael J. Moritz's Forms 3 and 4 for Nu Holdings Ltd. from SEC EDGAR, and the company's confirmation of what capacity he holds.** One document settles it. If those filings show him reporting as a **director**, then the FY25 20-F Item 6.A board table, the 2026 AGM nominee slate and the company's own investor-relations board page are all incomplete on the identity of the board — which would be a live disclosure-integrity finding on the most basic governance fact a company reports, and it would change A1-05, the A17-08 count and this module's disclosure-candor read at once. If they show him reporting as a >10% owner, an officer or in some other capacity, the conflict is a vendor attribution error and closes with no finding. It is the only open item in this file whose resolution could move a grade.

## 7. People & Network Integrity Read

Twenty-five named people and forty-three entities were swept, and the headline is that **the people who actually control this company are clean**: David Vélez — founder, chairman, chief executive and holder of 74.4% of the votes — his co-founder Cristina Junqueira, and the incoming CFO Rob Livingston returned nothing on any criminal, civil, securities-regulator, sanctions, disqualification, insolvency, credential or adverse-media axis, no undisclosed entity, and no cross-linkage; the controller's holding vehicle is named, quantified, 13G-reported and unpledged. The lineage question that triage correctly refused to pre-judge **closed clean on evidence**: the three-year gap between the 2013 founding claim and the 2016 Cayman incorporation resolves to Nu Pagamentos S.A. (CNPJ 18.236.120/0001-58, opened 4 June 2013), a disclosed, active, consolidated subsidiary that also owns the NUBANK marks — so there is no predecessor, no phoenix, no undisclosed former name, and no brand sitting outside the group.

**The riskiest node is not a person's own record — it is a linkage, and it sits on the wrong seat.** Rogério Calderón, chair of Nu's Audit and Risk Committee and its designated audit-committee financial expert, sat on the board and the audit and finance committees of Grupo Casas Bahia S.A., which filed for *recuperação judicial* over R$17.3 billion on about 16 August 2026 — three weeks before this report — and left that board in the same days. **Nothing adverse was found against him personally**; he joined that board in September 2019, the month the anonymous complaints that exposed its R$1.19bn accounting fraud arrived, so he was appointed into a clean-up rather than present for the failure, and his exit came *after* the filing, not ahead of it, which is why the "smart rat" test does not fire. But the proceeding is admitted, live and unresolved, so it is a Material-equivalent fact at a hop-1 entity: it floors his grade at Minor concerns, fires **RF-NET-003 band (b)**, and caps People & network integrity at 50. The second-order items are a KMP's own record — Campos Neto's Pandora-Papers-era offshore vehicles held while he ran Brazil's central bank, an unfavourable ethics-commission report terminated judicially rather than decided, and a six-month walk from regulator to regulated firm that the Brazilian government is now legislating to slow — and Douglas Leone's partnership at Sequoia Capital, a defendant in the pending, unadjudicated FTX investor class actions.

The discovery loop reached **hop 2** and stopped on `breadth_budget`, with sixty-five subjects named in the Scope-Boundary Register rather than dropped; it recovered one thing the filings' own governance section no longer shows — **Adam Edward Wible, Nu's third named co-founder** — and it identified the unnamed related-party counterparty as **Lightspark Group, Inc.**, David Marcus's company, from the matching Q2-2024 partnership date. **No §24 Filter 1 integrity signal is open:** `01_disqualifier-scan` routed nothing, an independent short-seller and forum sweep found nothing, and the one piece of partisan buzz that did surface (the Campos Neto union coverage) was chased to mainstream sources and resolved, so **RF-MGT-005 does not fire.**

**What a rational minority holder should conclude.** The people running Nu Holdings are not a reason to walk away — there is no crook here, no phoenix, no shadow network, no hidden brand, and no controller with a graveyard behind him, and the filings named almost everything we found. What a holder should hold onto instead are two specific, checkable things: that the board seat responsible for challenging the accounts is currently the seat carrying an unresolved insolvency exposure, three weeks old, and the board's response to it is not yet on the record; and that the company's public policy is now run by the man who wrote the rules it profits from, lawfully and after the required quarantine, but fast enough that Brazil is changing the rule. Neither fails the Non-Negotiable Gate. Both cap conviction, and both are exactly the kind of fact that looks small until the quarter it does not.

## management-governance / 08_audit-and-assurance-quality.md

_Source: `08_audit-and-assurance-quality.md`_

# Audit & Assurance Quality — NU

**Company:** Nu Holdings Ltd. (NYSE: NU) — Cayman Islands holding company, operating banks and payment institutions in Brazil, Mexico and Colombia.
**Regime (from triage `00`):** US SEC **foreign private issuer**. Annual filing = **Form 20-F** (not 10-K); interim = unaudited condensed statements furnished on 6-K; **no DEF 14A** — governance and auditor-fee disclosure sit in 20-F Items 6, 15 and 16A–16K. Reporting standard **IFRS Accounting Standards as issued by the IASB**; currency **US dollars, in thousands**; fiscal year ends **31 December**. Audit oversight: **SEC + PCAOB** at the listed level, **BCB / CMN** and **CVM** in Brazil, **CNBV** in Mexico, **SFC** in Colombia.
**Regime translation applied (CLAUDE.md §27):** India-specific items — CARO annexure (A4-11) and the MR-3 secretarial audit (part of A4-08) — do not exist in this regime. The PCAOB-form equivalents are used instead: Critical Audit Matters in place of KAMs, the ICFR attestation in place of the IFC annexure, and the SOX 302/906 certifications plus the BCB-mandated internal-controls officer in place of the secretarial compliance report. Where no local equivalent exists, the item is marked **Not Applicable (regime)** with the regime named — never left blank.

**Hard-lock deference (CLAUDE.md §13; MODULE_RULES Disqualifier Deference).** `business-model/01_disqualifier-scan.md` fired **no** audit-related hard lock. Quoted verbatim, test 1: *"Auditor qualification or going-concern note (last 3 years) — **N**. Unqualified opinion in all three years."* Test 4: *"Auditor changed twice in last 3 years without disclosed reason — **N**. Zero changes, let alone two."* Test 5: *"Material restatement (>5% of revenue or net income) in last 2 years — **N**. Computed: restatement amount = US$0."* Nothing below re-decides those calls; this report documents the full spectrum around them.

---

**One structural point up front.** A 20-F carries a **single** audit report on the **consolidated** statements. There is no standalone-versus-consolidated split to compare, because the SEC form does not produce one — so the usual "clean standalone, modified consolidated" tell cannot arise here. That is a feature of the regime, not a gap, and it is stated rather than scored.

| FY | Opinion (standalone) | Opinion (consolidated) | EoM / explanatory paragraph / going concern | IFC/ICFR opinion | Restatement / prior-period adjustment | Verdict | Source |

| FY2021 | n/a (regime — no standalone statements in a 20-F) | Unqualified | None; no going-concern doubt | **No auditor ICFR opinion — not yet required.** The 404(b) attestation box on the cover page is unchecked. **Management disclosed two material weaknesses**: (i) IT systems change-management processes and (ii) IT user identity and access-management processes | None | **Amber (historic)** | `FY21 Form 20-F (filed Apr-21-2022), cover page (404(b) box ☐); Item 3.D risk factors, p.23; Item 15` |
| FY2022 | n/a | Unqualified | None | **Unqualified — first ICFR attestation.** "we have remediated our previously disclosed material weaknesses as of such date" | None | **Green** | `FY22 Form 20-F (filed Apr-20-2023), Report of Independent Registered Public Accounting Firm; Item 15.B` |

Not a qualification and not an error correction | Unqualified | **A retrospective accounting-method change, not a restatement.** The cover-page error-correction box is unchecked | **Green, with the explanatory paragraph recorded** | `FY24 Form 20-F (filed Apr-16-2025), Report of Independent Registered Public Accounting Firm, p.F-3; Note 1(c)` |

"substantial doubt" appears nowhere; the only going-concern wording is the routine positive IAS 1 assertion in Note 2 | **Unqualified** — "the Company maintained, in all material respects, effective internal control over financial reporting as of December 31, 2025", COSO 2013 | **None.** Cover-page error-correction box ☐; Item 6.F: "We have not been required to prepare an accounting restatement at any time during or after our last completed fiscal year" | **Green** | `FY25 Form 20-F, Report of Independent Registered Public Accounting Firm, pp.F-3, F-6; cover page; Item 6.F; Item 15.B` |

**Plainly stated.** Every year FY2021–FY2025 carries a clean opinion on the consolidated financial statements, and every year FY2022–FY2025 carries a clean opinion on internal control over financial reporting (the systems that are meant to keep the numbers honest between audits). Vendor cross-check agrees for a longer window: opinion = "Unqualified" for FY2020 through FY2025 [`CIQ Auditors export (NU), FY2020–FY2026 window, data as of Aug-2026 — vendor export`]. The interim statements to 30-Jun-2026 carry a clean KPMG review conclusion dated 13-Aug-2026.

**The one wrinkle worth naming, because it is easy to lose.** Nu entered public markets **with two open material weaknesses in its IT controls** — change management and user identity/access. Management found them itself, more than a year before the IPO prospectus, and disclosed them; they were remediated by 31-Dec-2024… by **31-Dec-2022**, and KPMG's first ICFR attestation that same year was clean. That history is now four years old, was self-found and self-disclosed, and has not recurred. It does not fire a flag today. It is recorded because the weaknesses were in **IT access and change control** — the exact controls a digital-only bank depends on — and because a reader who only sees "clean ICFR, four years running" would not know it.

**Clawback.** A compensation clawback policy was adopted **2 October 2023** (Exhibit 97.1). Because no restatement has occurred, no recovery was required or pursued — the company says so directly, and the second cover-page box (error corrections requiring an incentive-compensation recovery analysis) is unchecked. Policy ownership is `03`'s item (A6-06); this row only records that the restatement trigger never fired.

## 3. Calibre, Rotation & Regulator Discipline (A4-01, A4-02, A4-13)

| Test | Raw value | Green band | Red band | Verdict | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **A4-01 — tenure vs local cap; rotation real?** | **8 fiscal years** (FY2018–FY2025), **zero** auditor changes. Item 16F "Change in Registrant's Certifying Accountant: **None**." US/SEC imposes no firm-rotation cap. Brazil's CMN Res. 4,910 caps the audit **firm** at 5 fiscal years, extendable to **10** where a statutory audit committee is in place — which it is | Terms compliant; rotation orderly and real | Same-network affiliate swap, or cap dodged via loopholes | **Green (compliant), with a dated forward constraint** | `FY25 Form 20-F, Item 16F, p.242`; `FY25 Form 20-F, audit report p.F-6 ("auditor since 2018")`; `FY25 Form 20-F, Item 4.B (CMN Res. 4,910 / BCB Res. 130)` |
| **A4-01 (b) — audit-team / lead-partner rotation** | **Cannot be verified.** Both regimes require the individual to rotate — SEC every 5 years for the lead partner, CMN Res. 4,910 every 5 consecutive fiscal years for the audit team. The 20-F **names no signing partner** in any of the five years read | Partner rotation evidenced | Same individual signing past the 5-year limit | **Insufficient Data** (coverage-limited: PCAOB Form AP AuditorSearch not reachable this run) | `FY25 Form 20-F, audit report p.F-6 (signed "/s/ KPMG Auditores Independentes Ltda.", no partner name)`; same in FY24, FY23, FY22, FY21 |
| **A4-02 — firm calibre vs company complexity** | Big-4 network member firm, PCAOB-registered (ID 1124), with a large Brazilian listed-company practice; the audit covers a **US$74.9bn**-asset group (FY2024: US$49.9bn) with **131 million customers** across Brazil, Mexico and Colombia. Firm size is not the issue; the firm's own regulatory record is (next row) | Big-4 / peer-reviewed national firm with a listed practice sized to this company | A firm too small for the complexity, **or a firm/partner with a disciplinary history** | **Amber** — sized for the job, but the red band's second limb is engaged by the discipline record below | `FY25 Form 20-F, consolidated statements of financial position (total assets US$74,893,877k at 31-Dec-2025; US$49,931,214k at 31-Dec-2024)`; `FY25 Form 20-F, Item 4.B (131 million customers as of December 31, 2025)` |
| **A4-13 — PCAOB / SEC / CVM / CFC orders vs firm or signing partner** | **Three live or recent matters against the FIRM in a 12-month window** (detailed below). None names Nu Holdings; none names an individual connected to this engagement — because no partner is named here | No orders against either | **Any active order or debarment** (also RF-AUD-007) | **Red — RF-AUD-007 (severity High, not Critical)** | Sweep Log rows SW-01 to SW-06 |

**Rotation: named, both sides.** There is nothing to compare, because there has been no rotation. KPMG Auditores Independentes Ltda. signed FY2018 through FY2025 and the FY2026 interim reviews. No incoming firm, no outgoing firm, therefore **no same-network affiliate swap** — the dodge this test exists to catch is absent. Item 16F says "None" and the vendor auditor history agrees for FY2020–FY2025.

**The forward constraint, dated.** CMN Res. 4,910's extended cap is **10 fiscal years**. Counting FY2018 as year 1, KPMG's tenth year at the Brazilian regulated entities is **FY2027** — meaning a **mandatory audit-firm change falls due from FY2028**, roughly two reporting cycles out, and no succession or tender process is disclosed anywhere in the pool. *Inference from the stated rule and the stated tenure, not a company disclosure.* Two caveats keep this honest: the "auditor since 2018" statement is made for **Nu Holdings Ltd.**, and the pool does not say when KPMG's clock started at **Nu Pagamentos** or **Nu Financeira** specifically (it could be earlier, which would pull the deadline forward); and the Cayman holdco's NYSE audit is not itself subject to any firm-rotation cap. Follow-up below.

**The discipline record, in full.** A Big-4 brand is not quality by itself, and here the brand is doing more work than the record supports:

1. **PCAOB, 11 March 2025 — settled disciplinary order, KPMG Auditores Independentes Ltda. censured** (one of nine KPMG network firms sanctioned the same day; **US$3.375 million** in total civil money penalties across the nine). KPMG Brazil faced the broadest set of charges of the nine: violating **Rule 3211** by failing to accurately disclose on **Form AP** the participation of other accounting firms — "including, among others, component auditors, shared service centers, and critical audit matter hubs"; violating **AS 1301** by failing to communicate to audit committees the **name, location and planned responsibilities** of one or more other accounting firms; violating **Rule 2200** by failing to report certain audit reports or consents on Form 2; and violating **quality control standards** on meeting professional standards and on monitoring. Settled without admitting or denying; remedial undertakings agreed. Press reporting attributes a **US$700,000** civil penalty to KPMG Brazil, though the firm-by-firm split is not stated in the PCAOB release or the law-firm summary, and one later report attributes that figure to KPMG Canada — so the **US$3.375m nine-firm total is the number I rely on**, and the per-firm figure is flagged as contested. [`Web: PCAOB news release, 2025-03-11 (dated, unverified)`; `Web: CFO Dive, 2025 (dated, unverified)`; `Web: King & Spalding client note (dated, unverified)`]
2. **PCAOB, 25 September 2025 — expanded inspection report published.** The PCAOB made public the previously non-public quality-control portion of an inspection report on KPMG Auditores Independentes Ltda. **because the firm did not address certain quality-control criticisms to the Board's satisfaction within the 12 months following the report date** (original report dated 6 July 2021). Publication of the Part II section is, by design, the sanction for failed remediation. [`Web: PCAOB inspection-report postings, 2025-09-25 (dated, unverified)`]
3. **CVM (Brazil), 20 May 2025 — settlement accepted (termo de compromisso), PAS CVM 19957.004339/2023-17**, concerning KPMG's audit of the Luggo real-estate investment fund for the year ended 30 June 2020. **KPMG Auditores Independentes Ltda. paid R$1,782,000 and the technical partner Anderson Luiz de Menezes paid R$99,000 — R$1,881,000 in total.** A Brazilian settlement carries no admission of guilt, but it does carry a payment obligation imposed by the securities regulator. [`Web: CVM news release, 2025-05-20 (dated, unverified)`]
4. **CVM — pending: PAS CVM 19957.004339/2023-17 is distinct from the Americanas matter.** A separate sanctioning proceeding was opened **26 November 2024** against KPMG and partner **Carla Bellangero** over the firm's audits of **Americanas S.A.** for FY2017–FY2018 — the retailer at the centre of one of Brazil's largest accounting frauds. The accusation document is not public and the case awaits judgment. An **allegation, not a finding** (MODULE_RULES: allegation ≠ conviction). [`Web: Brazilian press reporting of the CVM accusation, 2024-11-26 (dated, unverified)`]
5. **Two acquittals, recorded for balance.** CVM unanimously **acquitted** KPMG and partner João Alberto Dias Panceri on the Copel FY2015 audit (judged **2 September 2025**), and unanimously **acquitted** KPMG and partner Cláudio Rogélio Sertório on the Odontoprev FY2023 audit (judged **16 December 2025**). Both are exculpatory and are counted as such.

**Why High and not Critical.** The matters are against the **firm's practice-wide systems** — Form AP reporting, audit-committee communication, quality control — and one Brazilian fund engagement. **None names Nu Holdings, and none is a debarment.** Two of the four CVM matters ended in acquittal. Critical severity in this module is reserved for a proven fraud finding, a debarment, or an auditor fleeing the engagement, and none of those is present. But the flag fires, because "no orders against either" is plainly false and because the **specific** thing the PCAOB censured KPMG Brazil for — not disclosing which other firms participate in an audit, and not telling the audit committee about them — is exactly the disclosure an investor in Nu would need to answer Section 5 below, and cannot get.

**Coverage limit, stated.** The **signing partner is not named** in any year, so the A4-13 sweep could only be run against the **firm**. PCAOB AuditorSearch (Form AP), which does name the engagement partner, was not reachable this run. Any partner-level record — the one thing that would tell you whether the individual who signs Nu's numbers is among those named in the CVM matters above — is **unswept**. That is a coverage gap, not a clean result.

---

## 4. Economic Independence — Fees (A4-06, A4-07)

All figures **US$ thousands**, as printed. The prohibited-services list applied is **SOX §201** (US regime). India's Companies Act Sec 144 is **not applicable** here and is not used.

| FY | Audit fee | Audit-related | Tax | All other | Non-audit total (incl. network firms) | Non-audit / audit (%) | Prohibited services? | Fee vs benchmark | Revenue growth | Verdict | Source |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---|---|---|---|---|
| FY2024 | 1,928.3 | 48.6 | 5.2 | 6.5 | **60.3** | **3.1%** | None identified | — | — | **Green** | `FY25 Form 20-F, Item 16C, p.241 (2024 comparatives)` |
| FY2025 | **2,923.2** | 118.4 | 9.1 | 99.3 | **226.8** | **7.8%** | None identified | US$2.92m vs a **US$3.26m** average audit fee across 6,600+ SEC registrants in 2024 → NU pays **~90% of the all-filer average** | **+26.8%** (revenue US$5,513m → US$6,991m); total assets **+50.0%** (US$49.9bn → US$74.9bn) | **A4-06 Green; A4-07 Amber** | `FY25 Form 20-F, Item 16C, p.241`; benchmark `Web: Ideagen Audit Analytics audit-fee trend data for 2024, via TheCorporateCounsel.net, 2025-10 (dated, unverified)`; revenue `CIQ Financials→Income Statement (multi-year) — vendor export`; assets `FY25 Form 20-F, consolidated statements of financial position` |

**A4-06 — economic independence. Green.** Non-audit fees are **7.8%** of audit fees (US$226.8k against US$2,923.2k), far inside the 25% green band and nowhere near the red band of non-audit ≥ audit. The Enron pattern — Andersen earning more from consulting than from auditing — is absent by a wide margin. What the non-audit money bought is disclosed by category: audit-related work is accounting consultations, acquisition-related audits, internal-control reviews and non-statutory attest work; tax fees are compliance, advice and planning; and **"all other fees are fees billed for assurance services related to environmental, social and governance and sustainability assurance"** — that last line grew from US$6.5k to US$99.3k, which is a sustainability-assurance engagement starting up, not a consulting relationship forming. **None of the disclosed categories is on the SOX §201 prohibited list** (bookkeeping, financial-information-systems design, appraisal/valuation, fairness opinions, actuarial, internal-audit outsourcing, management or HR functions, broker-dealer or investment-banking services, legal and expert services). A pre-approval process exists and is described: every proposed engagement, audit and permitted non-audit alike, goes to the Audit and Risk Committee before it starts, per SOX and SEC rules, under a written policy posted publicly.

**One honest limitation.** Item 16C reports fees **billed to the company by "our independent registered public accounting firm"**. It does not separately itemise amounts paid to other **KPMG network firms** in Mexico or Colombia. The MODULE_RULES band requires network-firm fees to be included, and I cannot prove they are. If material amounts sat outside this table the ratio would rise — but for it to breach even the 25% green band, undisclosed network non-audit fees would have to exceed **US$504k**, roughly **2.2×** everything disclosed. Green stands; the limitation is on the record.

**A4-07 — fee level and trend. Amber, and the two halves point different ways.**

- **Trend: clean.** The audit fee rose **+51.6%** (US$1,928.3k → US$2,923.2k) while revenue rose **+26.8%** and total assets rose **+50.0%**. The fee is growing **faster than revenue and in step with the balance sheet it has to audit**. The red band this test exists to catch — a fee **falling** while revenue grows more than 20%, the signature of low-balling (pricing an audit too cheap to do it properly) — is the opposite of what happened.
- **Level: on the low side, and it deserves saying out loud.** US$2.92m buys the audit of a **US$74.9bn-asset** bank with **131 million customers** across three countries, an expected-credit-loss allowance of **US$5.0bn** estimated from internal scoring models, **and** a full ICFR attestation. That is **~90% of the US$3.26m average fee across more than 6,600 SEC registrants in 2024** — most of which are far smaller and simpler. The fee equals **0.042% of revenue**.
- **Why Amber rather than Red.** The red band is a fee **below 50%** of the peer median for the size band. I could not obtain a size-band peer median: an attempt to read Item 16C from Inter & Co's FY2025 20-F returned XBRL markup rather than narrative text, and no other LatAm digital-bank fee table is in the pool or was retrievable. The all-registrant average is a **cruder** benchmark than the band asks for, and NU sits at 90% of it rather than below 50%. Conservative default (§4) applied to the residual uncertainty: **Amber**, with the peer comparison marked coverage-limited.

| Nu Pagamentos S.A. — Instituição de Pagamento (Brazil) | Not disclosed | Not disclosed | **Not disclosed** | Unknown | `CIQ Corporate Structure Tree export (NU) — vendor export`; searched `FY25 Form 20-F` for a component-auditor reference: none |

S.F.P. / Nu BN México (Mexico) | Not disclosed | Mexico = **7%** of group revenue | **Not disclosed** | Unknown | geographic split `ciq_facts.json → geographic (12 months Dec-31-2025: Brazil 11,038 / 91%; Mexico 808 / 7%; Other 237 / 2% of 12,084) — vendor export` |

| Coverage measure | Raw value | Green band | Red band | Verdict | Source |
|---|---:|---|---|---|---|
| Principal auditor's share of consolidated assets/revenue (A4-14) | **100% by construction, 0% verifiable.** KPMG's report opines on "Nu Holdings Ltd. **and subsidiaries**" as a whole and **divides responsibility with no other firm** — under PCAOB AS 1206 that means the principal auditor takes responsibility for the entire consolidation. But the report does **not** state what share other firms performed, and the pool contains no Form AP data | ≥80% | <50%, or cash/revenue-rich components at unknown firms | **Amber** | `FY25 Form 20-F, Report of Independent Registered Public Accounting Firm, pp.F-3 to F-6 (single undivided opinion, no other-auditor reference)` |
| Material subs' auditor calibre (A4-03) | **No component auditor is disclosed for any of the 34 subsidiaries** — including the two Brazilian regulated entities that hold essentially all the group's assets and the Mexican bank that holds 7% of revenue | Parent auditor or comparable firms | Unknown firms, or components unaudited | **Amber** | Searched `FY25 Form 20-F` (all Items), `FY24`, `FY23`, `FY22`, `FY21` 20-Fs, and the CIQ Auditors export. The CIQ export lists **only** the parent ("Entity: Self") for FY2020–FY2025 — it contains no subsidiary auditor row |

**Writing the absence as the finding, as required.** Nu has **34 subsidiaries**, at least four of them regulated financial institutions across three jurisdictions, and **no component-auditor disclosure exists anywhere in the pool.** That absence is the answer to A4-03 and A4-14 — not a blank and not a routine N/A.

**Why Amber and not Red, and why it is not nothing.** The Wirecard/Satyam pattern the red band describes is a cash- or revenue-rich component sitting at an unknown local firm while the principal auditor quietly excludes it. **There is no evidence of that here**, and two structural facts push against it: KPMG's report is a **single undivided opinion** covering the whole consolidation, which under PCAOB standards means KPMG owns the work whoever performed it; and the entity holding the assets is a **BCB-supervised Brazilian bank**, itself subject to mandatory independent audit, internal audit and a statutory audit committee. So the coverage is very probably fine.

**But "probably fine" is not the same as verified, and there is a specific reason to press.** The disclosure that would let anyone check — PCAOB **Form AP**, which lists the other accounting firms participating and their share of hours, and the **AS 1301** communication of those firms' names and responsibilities to the audit committee — is **precisely what the PCAOB censured KPMG Auditores Independentes Ltda. for getting wrong on 11 March 2025**, across its practice, "including, among others, component auditors [and] shared service centers." The one control that would close this gap is the one the auditor's own regulator found defective. Investors cannot see it from the 20-F; the audit committee is supposed to be told, and its regulator says firms of this kind were not telling. That combination is what carries the item to Amber rather than Green, and it fires no red flag only because there is no affirmative evidence of an uncovered component. **RF-AUD-005 does not fire.**

| — | **Company secretary** | — | — | — | — | — | **No company secretary is named anywhere in the pool.** A Cayman FPI has no LODR-equivalent named-CS requirement; a change could not be observed either way |

**A4-04 — auditor resignation. Green, and cleanly so.** There has been **no** auditor resignation, mid-term or otherwise, in eight years. Item 16F reports "None". Every date test the band asks for therefore passes by default: there is no resignation to check against a limited-review calendar, none citing information access, unpaid fees or disagreements, and none following a qualification (there has never been a qualification). The reverse test also passes — KPMG signed the most recent interim review on 13 August 2026, four months into the current fiscal year, so the firm is still in the chair with its name on the current numbers. **RF-AUD-001 does not fire.**

**A4-15 — gatekeeper exit cluster. Amber, on a stated coverage limit rather than on an observed cluster.** On the strict test the answer is clean: the CFO changed, the **auditor did not**, so the CFO + auditor pairing that fires **RF-AUD-006 does not exist**, and the flag does not fire. The CFO handover has every marker the green band asks for — pre-announced, named successor, stated reason, a six-week overlap to 2026-08-31, and it coincides with no restatement, no auditor change and no qualified opinion.

Two things stop this being Green:
1. **Two of the four gatekeeper roles cannot be tracked.** Neither the **company secretary** nor the **head of internal audit** is named anywhere in the pool, so a CFO + CS or CFO + internal-auditor cluster could not be ruled out — it could only fail to be seen. Absence of observation is not evidence of absence (§3), and the conservative default applies to that residual gap alone.
2. **Two senior non-gatekeeper seats emptied in the same window with no announcement at all** — the **President & COO** (the company's number two, who had personally presented asset quality on the earnings calls) and the **CTO**, both between May and August 2025, neither explained, the President/COO seat not refilled. These sit outside A4-15's gatekeeper set and are `01`'s finding, not a second adjudication here. They are recorded because three senior seats — President & COO, CTO, CFO — reset inside roughly fifteen months, and a reader assessing whether the people who sign and check the numbers are stable should see that context. Nothing in the pool ties either exit to a financial, legal or accounting event.

## 7. KAM / CAM Recurrence (A4-10)

*(Regime note: a 20-F carries **Critical Audit Matters** under PCAOB AS 3101, the local equivalent of KAMs.)*

| KAM / CAM | Years it appeared | Underlying balance trend | Sector-standard or company-specific? | Verdict | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Expected credit losses on credit-card receivables and loans to customers** — the models, methods and assumptions behind probability of default, loss given default and exposure at default; the choice of macroeconomic variables (GDP, inflation, unemployment, the base interest rate); and the definition of a "significant increase in credit risk" (stage 2) | **FY2021, FY2022, FY2023, FY2024, FY2025 — five consecutive years, every year the company has been listed** | **Growing.** The allowance stood at **US$5,021,996 thousand at 31-Dec-2025**; the loan book behind it grew with a balance sheet that went from US$49.9bn to US$74.9bn of assets in one year | **Sector-standard for a lender** — the credit-loss estimate is the single largest accounting judgment in almost every bank's accounts — **but company-specific in its mechanics**, because the estimate runs off internal scoring models rather than observable prices | **Amber** | `FY25 Form 20-F, audit report pp.F-4 to F-5 (CAM, US$5,021,996k)`; `FY24 20-F (Apr-16-2025)`; `FY23 20-F (Apr-19-2024)`; `FY22 20-F (Apr-20-2023)`; `FY21 20-F (Apr-21-2022)` |
| **Value in use of the "Investment" cash-generating unit** — the discount rate and future growth assumptions in the impairment test | FY2022, FY2023, FY2024 — **and dropped in FY2025** | n/a — no longer a CAM | Company-specific (legacy of the Easynvest acquisition) | **Green — evidence the CAM set evolves** | `FY24 20-F, audit report`; `FY23 20-F`; `FY22 20-F`; absent from `FY25 20-F, audit report` |
| **Fair value of technology and customer-relationship intangibles acquired in the Easynvest acquisition** | FY2021 only | n/a | Company-specific, transaction-driven | **Green — appeared and resolved** | `FY21 20-F (Apr-21-2022), audit report` |

**The read.** Taken literally, the red band is tripped: the same high-risk matter — **receivables** — has recurred **five** years running while the underlying balance grew. Taken in context, it is not a wound the auditor keeps pointing at; it is the defining estimate of a consumer-lending business, and it would be more alarming if it were **not** a CAM. The MODULE_RULES regime-and-structure rule applies directly: do not flag a structure the business model dictates; judge the conduct within it.

Two facts decide the grade at **Amber** rather than Red or Green. Against Red: the CAM set **does** evolve — the Investment-CGU matter appeared for three years and was dropped in FY2025, and the Easynvest intangibles matter appeared once and resolved, so this is not a frozen boilerplate paragraph. In FY2025 the auditor also **deepened** its work on the recurring matter, bringing in credit-risk specialists to test the conceptual soundness of the models, re-check PD/EAD/LGD against historical data, and run regression analysis on whether the chosen macroeconomic variables actually correlate with credit risk. Against Green: five years and a growing balance is exactly the fact pattern the band was written for, and the estimate is model-based with no market price to check it against, which is why `11_accounting-forensics` — not this agent — owns the question of whether the provision is adequate. This row records the **audit** signal only.

## 8. CARO, Internal & Secretarial Audit (A4-08, A4-11)

**Local equivalents applied.** CARO 2020 and the MR-3 secretarial audit are creatures of the Indian Companies Act and SEBI LODR. **Neither exists for a Cayman-incorporated NYSE foreign private issuer**, and neither is marked as a data gap. The comparable local checks are: Brazil's mandatory internal-audit function for financial and payment institutions (CMN Res. 4,879 / BCB Res. 93), the mandatory internal-controls framework and designated internal-controls officer (CMN Res. 4,968, aligned to COSO 2013; BCB Res. 260 for payment institutions), and the SOX 302/906 certifications by the CEO and CFO.

| Test | Finding | Green band | Red band | Verdict | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **A4-11 — CARO annexure** | Does not exist in this regime. The nearest local equivalents — the auditor's ICFR opinion and the Brazilian internal-controls regime — are covered at A4-09 and below, and both are clean. There is **no** adverse finding on related-party loans, fund diversion, unrecorded transactions or undisclosed assets anywhere in the FY2025 audit report | Clean | Related-party loans, fund diversion, unrecorded transactions, benami items (RF-AUD-003) | **Not Applicable (regime — US/SEC foreign private issuer; no CARO requirement)** | Regime per triage `00`; searched `FY25 Form 20-F` audit report and Item 15 in full |
| **A4-08 (a) — internal audit function** | **Exists, is mandatory, and is overseen by the board committee — but the person running it is not named and nothing it found is disclosed.** Internal Audit is the "third line" and "periodically and independently evaluat[es] whether policies, methods and procedures are adequate, in addition to verifying their effective implementation." The Audit and Risk Committee's duties include "evaluating the performance, independence and progress of internal audit" and "ensuring management implements recommendations made by internal and independent auditors". Country-level audit committees perform the same function per local rules | Reputable internal auditor in place | No internal-audit function | **Amber** | `FY25 Form 20-F, Item 4.B (risk management — three lines; global and country-level governance bodies)`; `FY25 Form 20-F, Item 4.B (CMN Res. 4,879; BCB Res. 93)` |
| **A4-08 (b) — secretarial audit (MR-3) / local compliance-report equivalent** | No MR-3 requirement exists. The functioning local equivalents are present: **SOX §302 certifications by the CEO and CFO** (Exhibits 12.1, 12.2) and §906 certifications, a Code of Conduct and Whistleblower Policy applying to all employees, interns, officers and directors, and a Brazilian designated internal-controls officer under CMN Res. 4,968 / BCB Res. 260. **No individual is named as internal-controls officer** | Unqualified MR-3; peer-reviewed, shareholder-appointed; compliance report ≤60 days | Adverse/repeat remarks 2 yrs running, MR-3 absent where mandated, late/missing report | **Not Applicable (regime), with the local equivalents recorded as present** | `FY25 Form 20-F, Exhibit index (Exhibits 12.1, 12.2 — SOX §302 certifications)`; `FY25 Form 20-F, Item 16B (Code of Conduct, Whistleblower Policy)`; `FY25 Form 20-F, Item 4.B (CMN Res. 4,968; BCB Res. 260)` |

**Why A4-08 is Amber rather than Green.** The function unambiguously exists and is not optional — a Brazilian bank cannot lawfully operate without it, and the committee's charter puts internal audit's performance and independence squarely under its review. What is missing is anyone's name and any output. There is **no chief audit executive identified**, **no internal-audit headcount or budget**, **no summary of what internal audit found or whether management acted on it**, and **no named internal-controls officer** despite the Brazilian rule requiring one to be designated. A function whose leader cannot be named and whose findings are never summarised is a function an outsider must take entirely on trust. That is a disclosure shortfall, not evidence of a defective function — hence Amber, not Red.

## 9. Audit Committee ↔ Auditor Engagement (A4-12)

| Signal | Evidence | Verdict | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Private sessions** (committee meets the auditor **without** management present) | **Not disclosed either way.** Searched the FY25 20-F in full for "executive session", "private session" and "without management present" — **zero occurrences**. The Audit and Risk Committee charter, which would normally set this out, is on the company website and is **not in the pool**. A 20-F filer is not required to describe executive sessions, so silence here is expected rather than evasive. Per the A4-12 band, **mere silence is Insufficient Data, never Red** | **Insufficient Data** (disclosure-completeness note) | Searched `FY25 Form 20-F`, Items 6.C, 15, 16A–16G; `CIQ Committees export (NU) — vendor export` |
| **Auditor attendance and substantive engagement with the committee** | **Affirmatively evidenced, from both sides.** From the committee side: its duties include "appointing and overseeing the work and compensation of" the independent registered public accounting firm, "pre-approving the audit services and non-audit services", "evaluating the performance, independence and progress of … the independent external audit", and "reviewing and discussing the annual audited financial statements and unaudited quarterly financial statements **with management and the independent auditor**". It "meets at least quarterly". From the auditor's side: the critical audit matter is defined as a matter that "**w[as] communicated or required to be communicated to the audit committee**" — the auditor's own report confirms it talks to this committee about its hardest judgments | **Green** | `FY25 Form 20-F, Item 6.C (Audit and Risk Committee duties)`; `FY25 Form 20-F, Item 4.B (Audit and Risk Committee — "composed of three independent members and meets at least quarterly")`; `FY25 Form 20-F, audit report p.F-4 (CAM definition)` |
| **Independence of the committee's own advisory circle** *(routed to this agent by `01`)* | **A live question, and it is new.** From **2026-07-13**, the outgoing CFO **Guilherme Lago** — who signed the SOX certifications on five years of financial statements — became a **Special Advisor to the management team and to the Audit and Risk Committee**, advising on corporate development and strategy. He is **not a committee member**: the committee remains Calderón Peres, Sands and Pham, all three independent, chaired by the designated financial expert. No rule is broken. But the committee that is supposed to be the auditor's independent counterparty now has, as a standing adviser, the person who prepared the numbers it reviewed for five years | **Amber** | `CIQ Key Developments export (NU), "Executive Change – CFO", 2026-07-13 — vendor export`; `FY25 Form 20-F, Item 6.C (committee membership)`; routed from `management-governance/01_management-and-track-record.md, finding 01-007` |

**Answering the routed question directly, since `01` asked it.** *Does the ex-CFO's Special Advisor role to the Audit and Risk Committee compromise that committee's independence from management?* **On the evidence available: not as a matter of composition or of law — but it introduces a real conflict of interest that should be watched, and it lands at the worst possible moment.** Three points decide it. First, composition is untouched: all three members are independent, the chair is the financial expert, and an adviser has no vote — that part is `05`'s item (A2-01) and is unaffected. Second, the conflict is genuine and specific: a person who certified five years of accounts has an interest in those accounts not being reopened, and the audit committee is the exact forum where reopening would start. Third, the timing compounds it — the incoming CFO has **zero prior tenure at Nu** and his first full reporting cycle (Q3 2026, due ~2026-11-12) will be prepared under a finance organisation whose previous head now advises the body that reviews it. Nothing in the pool suggests misuse. But an audit committee's value is that the auditor and internal audit can speak to it about management **without management in the room**, and Nu discloses neither that such sessions happen nor any limit on the adviser's access. That is why the item is Amber with a follow-up, not a shrug.

## 10. Read

The chain that checks Nu's numbers is **able and, on the evidence, unafraid — but it is thinly lit.** Eight years with one auditor, five clean opinions on the accounts and four on the internal controls, no resignation, no restatement, no qualification, non-audit fees at 7.8% of audit fees with a working pre-approval policy, and an audit fee rising 51.6% while the balance sheet it covers rose 50.0% — none of that is bought, starved or scared off. The pre-IPO IT material weaknesses were found by management itself and closed in 2022.

**The single weakest link is not inside Nu — it is the auditor's own regulatory record, sitting on top of a disclosure Nu does not make.** In one twelve-month window KPMG Auditores Independentes Ltda. was censured by the PCAOB (11 Mar 2025) for practice-wide quality-control failings and for **not disclosing which other firms participate in its audits and not telling audit committees about them**; had the confidential quality-control section of a 2021 inspection report published (25 Sep 2025) for failing to remediate; and paid **R$1,782,000** to settle a CVM proceeding (20 May 2025). Meanwhile Nu discloses **no component auditor for any of its 34 subsidiaries**, and **names no signing partner in any of five years** — so neither the coverage of the consolidation nor the partner's disciplinary record can be checked at all. The one control that would close the first gap is the one the auditor's regulator says the firm got wrong. None of this is evidence that Nu's numbers are wrong; it is evidence that an outsider cannot independently confirm who audited what, or who signed it.

To trust these numbers more, three things would do it, in order: **(1)** the PCAOB Form AP for the FY2025 Nu audit, which names the engagement partner and every participating firm with its share of hours — swept against PCAOB and CVM records; **(2)** a statement that the Audit and Risk Committee meets the auditor and the head of internal audit **without management present**, and how often; and **(3)** disclosure of who runs internal audit and what it found. On top of that, a dated plan for the audit-firm succession that Brazil's ten-year cap makes due around FY2028.

**Conclusion: mixed — watch the named link (the auditor's own regulatory record combined with zero component-auditor visibility).**

## management-governance / 09_related-party-and-group-forensics.md

_Source: `09_related-party-and-group-forensics.md`_

# Related-Party & Group Forensics — NU

**Company:** Nu Holdings Ltd. (NYSE: NU) · Cayman Islands holding company, operations in Brazil, Mexico and Colombia
**Reporting regime:** SEC **foreign private issuer** → **Form 20-F** is the audited annual filing; **IFRS Accounting Standards**; presentation currency **US dollars**; fiscal year ends 31 December. Related-party accounting is **IAS 24**; the narrative regime is **Form 20-F Item 7.B**.
**Date of read:** 2026-09-06 · **Latest audited period:** FY2025 (20-F filed 2026-04-08) · **Latest interim:** H1 2026 (unaudited interim condensed financials, filed 2026-08-14)

All note figures below are **US$ thousands as printed** in the filings, restated to US$ millions only where compared against revenue, profit, assets or equity — the basis is labelled on every line.

---

## 1. RPT Intensity & the Applicable Regime (A5-01)

**Fix the regime first.** NU is **not** an Indian issuer, so **SEBI LODR Reg 23 does not apply** — neither the pre-Dec-2025 "lower of 10% of turnover or Rs 1,000 cr" line nor the Dec-2025 graded slabs. Naming them and setting them aside is the point of this step: applying either would be a bad-extraction error (CLAUDE.md §20, §27).

NU is also **not** subject to **Item 404 of Regulation S-K** and its US$120,000 disclosure floor. Item 404 binds domestic US registrants filing a 10-K / DEF 14A. As a **foreign private issuer**, NU discloses under:

| Layer | Rule that actually governs | What it requires | Where NU answers it |
|---|---|---|---|
| Narrative | **Form 20-F, Item 7.B** | Transactions with related parties **material to the company or to the related party** over the last three financial years; and **amounts outstanding on loans** to key management | `FY25 Form 20-F, Item 7.B (Related Party Transactions), p.205-206` |
| Financial statements | **IAS 24** | The **nature of the relationship**, the **amounts** of transactions and outstanding balances, and **key management personnel compensation** in aggregate. IAS 24 does **not** require the counterparty to be named | `FY25 Form 20-F, Note 28 (Related parties), p.F-77` |
| Approval | The company's own **Related-Party Transactions Policy** | "In March 2024, we updated our related party transaction policy, which requires certain related party transactions to be approved by our board of directors or a designated committee thereof, including our Audit and Risk Committee" | `FY25 Form 20-F, Item 7.B, p.206` |

**There is no majority-of-minority shareholder vote requirement in this regime, and none was held.** That is the rule, not a governance failure — but it also means the only check on an NU related-party transaction is a board / committee approval whose evidence is not published. That is scored at A5-07 below, not here.

### RPT intensity table

Denominators come from `earnings/01_historical-financials.md` (total revenue, net income to parent) and from the FY2025 20-F balance sheet (total assets US$74,893,877k; total equity US$11,321,562k) — used, not recomputed.

| FY | RPTs ex-dividends, **excl.** KMP comp (US$ k) | **Incl.** KMP comp (US$ k) | % of revenue (incl. comp) | % of PAT (incl. comp) | % of assets (incl. comp) | Material-RPT line that year | Above the line? | Minority-approved? | Verdict | Source |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---|---|---|---|---|
| FY2021 | 1,685 expense + 299 balance | 35,937 | 2.12% | n/m (net loss US$165.0m) | not computed | 20-F Item 7.B "material" test; no numeric floor | No | n/a (no FPI vote requirement) | Green | `FY21 20-F (filed 2022-04-21), Note 24` |
| FY2022 | 1,112 expense + 316 balance | 124,004 | 2.59% | n/m (net loss US$364.6m) | not computed | same | No | n/a | Green | `FY22 20-F (filed 2023-04-20), Note 25` |
| FY2023 | **nil** - "the Company did not have any transactions with other related parties" | 60,117 | 0.749% | 5.83% | not computed | same | No | n/a | Green | `FY23 20-F (filed 2024-04-19), Note 27` |
| FY2024 | 1,795 liability balance | 97,802 | 0.849% | 4.96% | not computed | same | No | n/a | Green | `FY24 20-F (filed 2025-04-16), Note 28` |
| **FY2025** | **926** liability balance | **92,195** | **0.58%** | **3.21%** | **0.123%** | same | **No** | n/a | **Green** | `FY25 20-F (filed 2026-04-08), Note 28(a)/(b), p.F-77` |
| H1 2026 (unaudited) | **265** liability balance | not separately disclosed for the half | 0.0014% on a TTM-revenue base - **mismatched, see note** | - | - | same | No | n/a | Green | `H1 2026 Interim Report (14 Aug 2026), Note 28(a)` |

**Arithmetic shown (FY2025).** 926 / 15,774,800 = **0.0059% of revenue**; 926 / 2,868,900 = **0.032% of PAT**; 926 / 74,893,877 = **0.0012% of assets**. Adding key-management compensation of 91,269: 92,195 / 15,774,800 = **0.58%**; / 2,868,900 = **3.21%**; / 74,893,877 = **0.123%**.

**Basis notes (CLAUDE.md §15).**
- The **926 / 1,795 / 265 figures are period-end BALANCES** (a liability), not flows. FY2025 and FY2024 disclose **no** related-party revenue or expense line at all - only the balance. So "% of revenue" sets a **point-in-time balance** against a **full-year flow**: the bases do not match. The matched version cannot be built because the company does not disclose the flow. Both bases are labelled inline every time the ratio appears, and **no monitoring threshold is derived from the unmatched ratio.**
- FY2021 and FY2022 figures **are** flows (revenues / expenses) and match the revenue denominator properly.
- The H1-2026 cell divides a 30-Jun-2026 balance by a trailing-twelve-month revenue figure. Mismatch labelled inline; shown only for direction of travel (1,795 -> 926 -> 265, falling), never as a share.
- The **% of assets** column pairs a FY2025 period-end balance with a FY2025 period-end asset base - that ratio **is** matched, and is the one clean ratio in this table.

**Verdict A5-01: Green.** On the strictest reading - every disclosed outside related-party item plus all key-management compensation, against consolidated revenue - related-party intensity is **0.58% of revenue in FY2025**, inside a Green band of <1-5%. Excluding compensation (remuneration is `03_incentives-and-compensation`'s subject, not a leakage channel), it is **0.0059%**.

**The >25% hard lock.** `business-model/01_disqualifier-scan.md` computed RP sales / revenue = 0.0% and RP purchases-expenses / total expenses = 0.76%, and returned **N**. My independent read reconciles: 91,269 / 12,032,723 total expenses = **0.76%**. **This module reports the ratio and defers to `business-model/01_disqualifier-scan` (hard lock) - it is not re-adjudicated here.**

**Why the note is short, and why that is structure rather than opacity.** Note 28 gives the mechanical reason: "all entities within the Group are consolidated in these consolidated financial statements. Therefore, related party balances and transactions, as well as unrealized gains or losses arising from intercompany transactions, are eliminated" [`FY25 20-F, Note 28, p.F-77`]. Every entity in the group is majority- or wholly-owned and fully consolidated. There is **no associate, no joint venture and no equity-method entity** through which value could move without appearing in the consolidated numbers, and **no promoter operating company** anywhere in the picture. A short RPT note in a wholly-consolidated single-controller group with no promoter trading entities is the expected shape. The partial-data rule is therefore **not** triggered: the related-party note exists, in all five years, in English, audited.

---

## 2. The RPT Ledger (every named counterparty, all five years)

This is the complete list of every outside related counterparty NU has disclosed since it became a public filer. Amounts in **US$ thousands as printed**. Positive = asset; brackets = liability or expense.

| Counterparty | Relationship | Type | FY2021 | FY2022 | FY2023 | FY2024 | FY2025 | H1 2026 | Trend | Arm's-length basis disclosed? | Source |
|---|---|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---|---|---|
| **Rodamoinho Produtora de Eventos Ltda.** | Owned by a **then-member of the Board of Directors**; ceased to be a related party in **September 2022** when that director left the board | Service and naming-rights agreement entered **2021-06-30** (expense) | (1,685) combined | (1,112) combined | nil - relationship ended | - | - | - | Ended | **No** - no methodology, no benchmark, no approval evidence given | `FY21 20-F, Note 24`; `FY22 20-F, Note 25`; `FY23 20-F, Note 27` |
| **Reprograma** | "a philanthropic project managed by a **family member of the Company's controlling shareholder**" | Payments for training and workshops - 2021-01-27, 2022-04-12, 2022-07-15 | included above | included above | nil | - | - | - | Ended | **No** | `FY21 20-F, Note 24`; `FY22 20-F, Note 25` |
| **Company's Board Members** (unnamed, as a class) | Directors | Purchase of **240,072 Series G-1 preferred shares at US$39.988768/share**, "for a total amount of US$1,600" | 1,600 as printed | - | - | - | - | - | One-off, pre-IPO | Priced at a stated per-share price; **no independent valuation disclosed** | `FY21 20-F, Note 24` |
| **Unnamed - "a company where one of its Directors serves as CEO"** (identified below as **Lightspark Group, Inc.**) | Counterparty whose CEO is an NU independent director (**David Alexandre Marcus**) | Commercial relationship entered **Q2 2024**; NU **received** a cash incentive to support integration project costs, held as a liability pending satisfaction of conditions | - | - | - | **(1,795)** | **(926)** | **(265)** | Unwinding as conditions are met | **No methodology disclosed**; only the standing "similar terms" boilerplate, which does not even attach to this item | `FY24 20-F, Note 28(a)`; `FY25 20-F, Note 28(a) fn.(i), p.F-77`; `H1 2026 Interim, Note 28(a)` |
| **Executive directors, board members, key employees and close family members** (unnamed, as a class) | KMP and close family | **Credit cards, loans, deposits and other products** issued in the ordinary course | **not quantified** | not quantified | not quantified | not quantified | not quantified | not quantified | Unknown | Assertion only: "on similar terms as those offered to unrelated third parties under similar circumstances and do not involve more than the normal risk of collectability" | `FY25 20-F, Note 28, p.F-77` (identical wording all five years) |
| **Key management personnel** (aggregate) | KMP | Fixed and variable compensation | 34,252 | 122,892 | 60,117 | 96,007 | **91,269** | not disclosed for the half | Down 5.0% YoY in FY2025 | n/a - remuneration, not a trade | `FY25 20-F, Note 28(b), p.F-78` |

### Three things this ledger says that the headline number does not

**1. The Note 28(a) counterparty is Lightspark Group, Inc. — verified independently, and the identification holds.** I did not take `07_people-integrity-dossiers`' conclusion on trust; I re-read the note text myself. Note 28(a) fn.(i) reads, verbatim: *"In the second quarter of 2024, Nu entered into a commercial relationship with a company where one of its Directors serves as CEO. As part of this agreement, Nu received a cash incentive, which will be used to support projects costs upon the Company's satisfaction of certain conditions"* [`FY25 20-F, Note 28(a) fn.(i), p.F-77`]. Four facts have to coincide, and they do: (i) exactly **two** NU directors are sitting CEOs — David Marcus of Lightspark and Jacqueline Reses of Lead Bank [`FY25 20-F, Item 6.A`]; (ii) the **Nubank-Lightspark partnership was announced 2024-06-25 = Q2 2024**, matching the quarter in the note (web sweep 2026-09-06, first-party company newsroom and PRNewswire); (iii) the **direction of payment** is *to* NU — a partner start-up paying an integration incentive to a bank with 100m+ customers is the commercially sensible direction, the reverse is not; (iv) the stated use, **"support project costs"**, matches a technical integration. `07`'s sweep found **no NU-Lead Bank transaction**. This is an **inference from four matching facts, labelled as such (CLAUDE.md §3)** — the filing does not name the counterparty. Confidence: high, not certain.

**2. The single largest disclosed number in this ledger flows the WRONG way for a leakage thesis.** The 926 is a **liability of NU** — money NU *received* and has not yet earned. Over three periods it has run down 1,795 -> 926 -> 265 as conditions were satisfied. There is no year in which NU **paid** an outside related party anything larger than the roughly US$1.1-1.7m of Rodamoinho and Reprograma costs in 2021-2022, both of which ended more than three years ago.

**3. One printed figure in the FY2021 note does not tie, and it has never been repeated.** The note states NU "sold 240,072 Series G-1 preferred shares at a purchase price of US$39.988768 per share to the Company's Board Members, for a total amount of US$1,600." At the stated price, 240,072 x 39.988768 = **US$9,600 thousand**, not US$1,600 thousand — a factor of six. In a statement presented in US$ thousands, the printed total does not reconcile to the printed price and quantity. I record it as an **unreconciled figure in the FY2021 note**, materiality **Low** (either reading is under US$10m against a company that has since earned US$2.9bn in a year), never repeated in FY2022-FY2025, and I do **not** silently pick whichever number suits. It is an accuracy observation on a five-year-old pre-IPO disclosure, not a leakage finding. [`FY21 20-F, Note 24`]

**Unnamed "entities where KMP exercise influence" carrying material value: none.** The one unnamed counterparty carries **US$0.926m** — 0.0059% of revenue. That is not a material unnamed exposure. **A5-08 is graded on disclosure practice below, not on this amount.**

---

## 3. Promoter-Linked Channels

### 3A. Royalty / brand / technology fees (A5-02)

| Payee | What is provided | Amount | % of turnover | Basis disclosed? | Trend vs margins | Prior minority approval? | Verdict | Source |
|---|---|---:|---:|---|---|---|---|---|
| **None** | - | **nil** | **0.00%** | n/a | n/a | n/a (no FPI requirement; none needed) | **Green** | `FY25 20-F, Note 28 (no royalty, brand or technology-fee line exists)`; Statements of income, cost lines |

**The brand-ownership question, answered rather than assumed (A5-02 x A17-04).** The rule that matters here is not "is there a royalty line" but "who owns the marks the company trades under, and is the licence priced?" `07_people-integrity-dossiers` ran the trademark-registry check and I adopt its finding after checking its basis: **NUBANK (USPTO serial 86386363) and NU BANK (serial 86963402) are registered to NU PAGAMENTOS S.A. - INSTITUICAO DE PAGAMENTO**, a wholly-owned, fully consolidated subsidiary named in Note 3 [USPTO via Justia Trademarks, read 2026-09-06; `FY25 20-F, Note 3, p.F-19`].

The marks therefore sit **inside the consolidated group** - not with a controller vehicle, not licensed in from outside, not in dispute. There is consequently **nothing to price**: no licence fee is disclosed because none is owed to anyone outside the consolidation, and an intra-group licence would be eliminated in consolidation anyway. This is the one case where "no fee disclosed" is the correct answer rather than the finding.

**RF-NET-004 does not propagate.** The registry's ADVERSE conditions are none of them met: the owner is not controller-linked; there is no external licence whose terms, fee basis or duration could be undisclosed; there is no licence in dispute or terminable at short notice; and no unrelated live company was found using the marks in an overlapping class. External brand ownership alone would not have fired it in any case, and here there is not even external ownership.

**One adjacent brand payment, correctly outside this table.** NU holds the naming rights to the Palmeiras arena in Sao Paulo (the "NeoQuimica"/"Allianz"-class deal, announced publicly). That is a **payment by NU to an unrelated sports club** - a marketing cost, not a related-party royalty. It is named here only because the FY2021-22 Rodamoinho item was *also* a naming-rights agreement, and the two must not be conflated: Rodamoinho was related-party (a director's company) and ended in 2022; the arena deal is arm's-length and current.
